prompt: Which of these use only **O(1) auxiliary space**, a constant amount however long the list of n items is (are in-place)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reversing a list with two swapping pointers
options.explanation: Correct. It needs just two indices and a temporary for the swap, whatever the length.
Not in place. The slice allocates a brand-new list of n elements.
Correct. `list.reverse()` reverses the list in place and returns None; it does not allocate a new list.
Not in place. Merging needs an O(n) temporary buffer (on top of an O(log n) recursion stack). Here n is the input size or recursive argument stated in the question.
Correct. Heapsort builds the heap inside the array itself and needs only a constant number of extra variables.

workedExample: Check whether extra storage grows with the list length n. Two-position swapping, list.reverse and iterative heapsort use constant auxiliary words. A reversed slice creates a new list. Standard array merge sort needs a linear merge buffer. Mutation alone does not establish an in-place space bound.

prompt: Your quicksort picks the first element as pivot and recurses on both partitions. On a sorted input of 100,000 items it crashes with a stack overflow. Which change guarantees O(log n) stack depth (proportional to the base-2 logarithm of the number of items n) **even in the worst case**, without changing the pivot rule?

options.explanation: This might avoid the error, but the depth is still Θ(n) and each frame still costs memory. It treats the symptom, and deep enough input will still crash. Here n is the input size or recursive argument stated in the question.

options.text: Recurse on the left partition first, then the right
options.explanation: Order alone does not change depth: sorted input gives an empty side and another only one item smaller, so the recursive chain still grows linearly with item count.

options.text: Recurse only on the smaller partition and handle the larger one with a loop
options.explanation: Correct. Every extra recursive frame receives at most half the current items; the larger partition is handled by a loop.

options.text: Switch the partition step to use a temporary list
options.explanation: That adds O(n) extra space per level and does nothing about recursion depth. Here n is the input size or recursive argument stated in the question.

workedExample: Each newly created frame must receive the smaller partition, which is at most half the parent’s size. Handle the larger partition by updating bounds inside a loop. This gives logarithmic maximum stack depth in item count n. Merely changing call order does not shorten the chain. The poor pivot can still produce quadratic total work.
